newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: PRICING KEY TO S.AFRICA PURCHASES OF ASIAN CRUDE.
newsitem.headline: PRICING KEY TO S.AFRICA PURCHASES OF ASIAN CRUDE.

text.p: Price and quality will determine whether South African oil buyers switch to southeast Asian crude following President Nelson Mandela's successful tour of the region, industry sources said on Thursday.
South African oil companies have traditionally sourced most of their crude from the Middle East, notably Iran, although they have now started buying Iraqi crude under the U.N. oil for food agreement.

Mandela and Minerals and Energy Affairs Minister Penuell Maduna have said several times during the tour the country could buy oil from the region while seeing more investments from the region in petrochemical projects in South Africa.
"If the economics and the quality work out, we could buy from Malaysia or Brunei," one trader told Reuters.
But another source said that Malaysian oil would probably not be ideally suited to South Africa in terms of yields, pricing and economics.

"As far as I am aware, they tend to be loaded in small parcels and the shipping and freight economics of small parcels would probably not be competitive unless there is some below the usual market figure traded," he said.
"At current market indications, it would not be attractive to us."
He said the situation was probably similar for oil from Brunei.

"There is quite a demand for these crudes within their local trading areas, so it is not as though they sit with cargoes that are readily available for moving long distances around the world," another source said.
Southeast Asia was further from South Africa than Middle Eastern oil fields, which would affect freight costs, although a lot depended on the loading capacity of ships used.

"So far they have appeared not to be attractive to use but it is the sort of thing one reviews regularly and if the ministers are talking, it will be super if something comes to the table and we will evaluate it on an economic basis," the source said.
Meanwhile, Caltex is still waiting to test the quality of the first crude oil cargo of Basrah Light which recently arrived off Saldanha Bay.
"We are not expecting any surprises but we should have a clearer idea of quality by the end of the month," a spokesman said.

"It is a crude we have run before and it is very suitable to our refinery. We will run this through our refinery just to make sure that there are no substantial changes from the quality that it is claimed to be."
